stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Published 19 November 2026

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next Published 1 day ago

Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? Published 4 days ago

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left Published 2 days ago

An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , external , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".

He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".

"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

stories.title: Fine Gael leader wants border poll criteria talks with London
stories.summary: Simon Harris says a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027

Published 19 November 2026

The leader of Fine Gael, Simon Harris, has said that a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful".

Harris, who is the tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minister), said he and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin are "aligned" on the issue.

He said there could be joint Irish government proposals on Irish unity preparation "by the end of the year".

It comes after the Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said that it is his job to decide when to bring forward a border poll and that he does not "detect a mood" for it.

Harris said that it would be good if the British and Irish governments "could at least have a shared understanding as to what criteria may be considered".

"At a point in time Dublin and London having a conversation about criteria is useful and is also just good governance," he said

Speaking on BBC News NI's The View programme, he added: "British Irish relations have never been better".

Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State, decides whether to call a border poll or not.

On Thursday morning Sir Chris told RTÉ's Morning Ireland programme , external he would "only bring forward a border poll at such time" as he thinks the people of Northern Ireland would want to join a united Ireland

"I don't detect that that is the situation now," he added.

Asked what criteria he will use to decide if the mood to join a united Ireland appears likely, he said "when it appears likely".

Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State decides whether to call a border poll or not

When asked why the Irish government should not have a role, Sir Chris said that the Good Friday Agreement is very clear that it's a matter for the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and that is agreed by the two governments as co-guarantors.

In response, the tánaiste said that "the commitment in the Good Friday Agreement is exactly as Chris Bryant read out, there's no disputing of that. But the application of that is something that would be good to have a greater understanding".

Simon Harris sent a letter to some party leaders in Northern Ireland asking for their views after his party, Fine Gael, published proposals on how to prepare for Irish unity .

The "blueprint" on Irish unity came days after the taoiseach, leader of Fianna Fáil, circulated a document to his parliamentary party laying out his own thoughts on how to prepare for a united Ireland .

He proposed setting up a new "initiative" on the constitutional future of the island of Ireland.

The two parties are both in a coalition government, supported by a number of Independent TDs (members of the Irish parliament) in Dublin.

Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027, under the coalition's rotating taoiseach agreement.

He added that he had already had discussions with the Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

'Equal' constitutional futures

Harris said that people don't need to agree with the outcome to wish to partake in discussions on Irish unity.

"We no longer live on an island where one constitutional view has greater value than the other. We left that behind us as a people when we voted for the Good Friday Agreement,"he said.

"Both views are legitimate and just like nationalists have lived in a Northern Ireland that has been part of the United Kingdom, it is possible in the future that unionists will live in a Northern Ireland that is part of a united Ireland."

"In both scenarios it's important that we have good relations. It's important that we are respectful, inclusive and we are willing to engage."

What's in Harris' 'blueprint'?

Among their proposals, Fine Gael has suggested appointing a junior minister in the Irish government for "north south relations".

The party also published a document by an economist who works as an adviser to Harris, where it was suggested that the first-year cost of reunification ranges from about €3bn (£2.5bn) to €25bn (£20.8bn) to the Irish exchequer.

His party has now proposed setting up an "independent, government-supported, inter-party and consultative forum" as part of preparations for reunification of the island.

The forum would look at the "future" of the institutions in Northern Ireland and the "possible subsequent reform of local and regional government on an all-island basis in line with the European principle of subsidiarity".

It would also examine the changes needed in Ireland's institutions, as well as public taxation, healthcare, education and other public services and practical requirements.

What has the political reaction been?

Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill said she welcomed the tánaiste's call for clarity on the criteria for a referendum on Irish unity adding "the British Government cannot continue to ignore the historic change on our island".

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said that his party was "not interested in self-harm and conversations that would see the end of the UK as we know it".

Alliance leader Naomi Long has said that her party will "engage respectfully" in any conversations about Northern Ireland's future.

The SDLP leader Claire Hanna welcomed the letter and said "a New Ireland must mean precisely that: an opportunity to build a new nation, not simply reverse partition".

Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows, described Fine Gael's plans as a "constitutional pet project" and said his party "will not participate in any project designed to dismantle the United Kingdom".

In his response to Harris, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said his "courtship techniques are somewhat lacking".

In response to unionist concerns, Harris said that "they are absolutely entitled to disagree" but that he "would never call their view in relation to the constitutional status fairy-tale or dangerous and all I would ask in respectful debate that they would too".

Analysis

Simon Harris may have stopped short of demanding the British government publish the criteria for a border poll but this is a nudge in that direction.

He, like his partner in government Michael Martin, is keen to flush out what the threshold for a poll might look like.

But they know there is little chance of that happening anytime soon.

Setting out the criteria for a border poll would result in the British government surrendering control of the process and that is something it is not prepared to do.

There is no desire to be tied to a threshold beyond its control.

So while unionists will argue this latest Harris intervention hasn't brought the prospect of a united Ireland any closer, it has injected more momentum into the wider unity conversation.

And the prospect now of a joint Dublin government proposal on Irish unity will energise the debate even more.

The Taoiseach and Tánaiste are no longer spectators in the stand, they are now players on the pitch and it feels like game on.

stories.summary: Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali is in hospital with serious injuries.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ibrar Ali was attended by emergency services on Manse Street in Bradford

Published 19 November 2026

A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.

Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.

West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.

The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".

Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.

A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was stabbed while walking around Bradford Moor

Ahmed said Ali was undergoing emergency surgery at Leeds General Infirmary after being stabbed in the leg. He said Ali was in a stable condition but had lost a lot of blood.

"My thoughts are with him and his family and loved ones. It's an extremely distressing time," said Ahmed.

"We shouldn't have to fear for our personal safety because we have chosen to serve the public.

"There should be no normalisation of violence in our democratic life."

Responding to the incident in his Bradford East constituency, Labour MP Imran Hussain described the incident as "horrific" and "deeply disturbing".

"My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family," said Hussain.

"No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community."

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked on Manse Street

Ch Supt Richard Padwell urged anyone with information to contact police.

"This is a serious incident where a local councillor has been stabbed in the street and our thoughts are with him, his family and colleagues at this difficult time," he said.

"Whilst the investigation is in the early stages, there is nothing to suggest that this incident is politically motivated at this time."

Ali is a community development manager at charity The Leap.

He has worked with community organisations Bradford Moor Pass and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

He was first elected as a councillor in the May local election, replacing the previous Labour representatives.

Councillors from across the political spectrum offered their support to Ali.

A spokesperson from the Reform UK group said they were "deeply saddened and shocked".

"At times like these, we come together as colleagues and as a community to support one another," they said.

Councillor Imran Khan, leader of Bradford Labour group, said he was "horrified" by the attack.

"All politicians, regardless of political affiliation, should be able to perform their role safely and without fear, threat of violence, or intimidation," he said.

Rebecca Poulsen, leader of the Conservative group added: "We were appalled to hear of this incident and wish Cllr Ali a full and speedy recovery."

Outside of Bradford, councillors from across West Yorkshire said they stood in "solidarity" with colleagues.

Leeds City Council leader James Lewis said he was "was shocked and deeply saddened to hear of the attack".

"Councillors of all parties play a vital role in serving their communities and should be able to carry out their duties without fear of violence or intimidation," he said.

Kirklees councillor, Tim Bamford, said the attack on Ali had been "very worrying".

"It's very worrying because if we're out campaigning or leaflet dropping we do get a level of abuse – nothing violent – but there's a lot of rhetoric out there and there is some abuse directed towards councillors," he explained.

US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.

The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .

White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.

“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.

“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.

Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.

Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.

“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.

Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.

“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .

Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

stories.body:
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.

Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea , the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.

The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping . As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.

From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.

For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China , the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.

The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and the USSR sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”

Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.

Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.

It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.

By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.

Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”

It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.

For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

stories.summary: A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said . “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable

Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said . “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there.

Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.

We tend to think of government as being authoritarian, democratic or somewhere in between. For the last 22 months, we’ve witnessed what happens when the US government turns authoritarian.

An economy can also be described along the same continuum.

Throughout most of the last century, the US economy was fairly democratic. Decisions about what was produced and at what price reflected the judgments of tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers and small-business owners – all of whom were trying to respond to consumers and investors. Through labor unions, workers also had some say.

But the US economy has become far more authoritarian.

In recent decades, it’s become concentrated in the hands of a few giant corporations. Economies of scale have enabled those corporations to spread their fixed costs over many goods and services, and the US government has nearly abandoned antitrust (anti-monopoly) enforcement.

Labor unions have shrunk from representing over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s to just 6% today.

More recently – over the last five years – something else has occurred, especially in big tech, that’s pushed the economy much further toward authoritarianism.

A handful of men – among them, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang – have not only become the richest people in the world, with significant political clout. They also control the direction and pace of technologies on which the US and the world depend.

These men are, in fact, the authoritarians of the new economy. They have unparalleled power over every aspect of the lives of Americans and millions of others around the world. And they have leveraged themselves to be, or seem, too big to fail.

The leverage works like this.

Nvidia’s value depends on Jensen Huang.

Hours after Huang’s resignation last Thursday, Nvidia stock dropped 10.3% in pre-market trading, erasing approximately $490bn of Nvidia’s value by the time the market opened.

Since the start of the leadership controversy at Nvidia on 8 November, the company has lost about $800bn in market value.

The AI industry, in turn, depends on Nvidia. Nvidia controls about 90% of the global market share of advanced AI chips. It has also become the major financier for the entire AI industry. Some call Nvidia the “ central bank of AI ”.

Nvidia’s $5tn market value (before 8 November) equaled about 8% of the total value of the S&P 500.

The US economy, in turn, depends on the AI industry. In the first quarter of 2025, the buildouts of datacenters using Nvidia chips accounted for 92% of US economic growth. Over the past two years, AI has been responsible for roughly half of America’s overall growth.

This huge leverage also works in reverse. Analysts fear that Nvidia’s collapse could cause the AI bubble to burst, triggering a failure that could threaten the entire US, if not also the world, economy.

Most Americans’ 401(k)s are invested in giant index funds tied to the Nasdaq and S&P 500. The Nasdaq and S&P 500, in turn, are based largely on 10 huge corporations . These 10 corporations are all connected to Nvidia. Together, they comprise about 37% of the value of the entire US stock market.

What all this means is Jensen Huang may be too big to fail.

More than 177,000 people have so far signed a “Stand with Jensen” open letter demanding that Nvidia’s board of directors “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Signers include Elon Musk; the Y Combinator president, Garry Tan; the Epic Games CEO, Tim Sweeney; and thousands of self-reported Nvidia employees.

Huang is discussing a possible return to the company, though the chair of the company’s board has said it’s not considering the move . One Huang ally talks of a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return, ‌and garner support from ‌Trump. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person told the Financial Times, adding that the efforts have Huang’s support.

Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as Nvidia CEO, adding that he thought Huang had “learned a big lesson”.

Exactly what “big lesson” did Trump have in mind? That it’s not a good look for the CEO of the US’s most valuable corporation to have a romantic relationship out of wedlock?

Or that such a CEO shouldn’t break the law by supplying America’s most advanced AI chips to China through a Chinese spy?

On Tuesday, it was announced that Huang has agreed to appear on 1 December before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee in transcribed interviews.

Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he? We may soon find out.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“H istoric” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

Mr Trump has got a red carpet embrace, another “first” to promote – preferable to headlines dwelling on the Republicans’ midterms disaster – and the congenial company of strongmen. His nation has less to celebrate. Mr Trump seems to see meeting longstanding US allies as at best a chore. His bruising tariffs and nakedly transactional approach to security, as well as his love of autocrats, have pushed countries like the Philippines – which hosted the US president en route to China – into hedging their bets.

Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage – perhaps not least because his closeness to Jensen Huang, the company’s ousted CEO, makes the issue at least as discomfiting for him as it is for Beijing. The US president is unlikely to embarrass the two countries that are central to Iran’s ability to resist his disastrous and illegal war, or to press China over its facilitation of Russia’s war against Ukraine . Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious any time he speaks to Mr Putin and Mr Xi. But the US president is as likely to undermine them, whether deliberately or otherwise, in bilaterals or via a throwaway remark.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta summit of Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill – which divided up Europe – grotesquely overstate the importance of a meeting scheduled to last less than an hour. Mr Xi does not do spontaneity, and is unlikely to be lured into sudden announcements. And despite the surface amity, the three still have strongly competing interests. China’s threat to rare earths brought a trade truce, but skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation . While China is arming itself at worrying speed, its arsenal is still dwarfed by those of the US and Russia.

Talking to rivals and adversaries is not inherently unwise. Under another US president, a closely focused and carefully prepared trilateral on, for instance, disarmament might even be fruitful. This is not that world. This will not be that meeting.

stories.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
stories.summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance Published 22 hours ago

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Several buildings were damaged in the latest Russian attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

stories.body:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.

As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

stories.title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
stories.summary: People who signed up to a government insulation scheme have been struggling to get their damaged homes repaired.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ken Palfrey is among the home owners waiting for repairs to faulty insulation

Published 19 November 2026

More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.

The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.

Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.

He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.

McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".

Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.

The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.

Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.

He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.

He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.

He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.

Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".

Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business.

"It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said.

"Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."

A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme".

"We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.

'Failures in the system'

Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".

But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".

When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.

He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."

He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".

A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."

The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality".

"Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added.

"When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."

Ken Palfrey said his external home insulation was "botched"

The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).

ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.

GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.

The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.

Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes.

"Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action.

"Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes.

"The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."

A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down.

"No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case.

"Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

stories.title: PM urges social media companies to 'show some decency' and take down Brand video
stories.summary: The comments came after YouTube owner Google refused a government request to remove a clip posted by the wife of the jailed comedian in which he claims he is innocent.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 November 2026

Social media companies should "show some decency and take these videos down", the prime minister has said, following a government attempt to have a YouTube video featuring a message from the jailed comedian removed.

The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Speaking following a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Andy Burnham said it was "time that we focus on the victims and think about them," rather than "hearing from a convicted criminal".

He said: "I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. Why are we having to hear from him. We shouldn't be and certainly [victims] shouldn't be hearing from him."

But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.

"Show some decency and take these videos down."

Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Laura Brand shared a video on their Sunday Service channel on the website and read out a message from her husband in which he said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be removed, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says Published 3 days ago

Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message Published 2 days ago

Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand Published 10 November

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.

"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."

However, the BBC understands there are no new plans to update or bring fresh legislation governing online platforms as a result of Brand's case.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".

Badenoch told Today, YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".

"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.

Connie Shaw of the Free Speech Union backed Badenoch's comments, saying that "if we want to protect everyone's free speech, we have to protect the free speech of even the most heinous people".

Speaking to the BBC's Politics Live, she said that it would "set a very dangerous precedent if we said that Russell Brand's wife is not able to express the fact that he rejects the fact that he has been found guilty".

Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".

Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.

In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.

"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."

The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.

Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.

"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

Additional reporting by Steven McIntosh and political correspondent Harry Farley

stories.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street last month

Published 19 November 2026

The UK will provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones to target Russia beyond the front line, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced.

The drone support was announced at a meeting in Berlin of Ukraine's allies, the Coalition of the Willing, and is part of a new £260m package to boost its war defences this winter.

The government said the drones are able to fly up to 625 miles (1,000km) and carry heavier warheads, enabling Ukraine to target military production facilities.

The move is the latest sign of a growing British involvement in drone technology for Ukraine. The government said 80% of the package will be spent in the UK.

The Berlin talks came as US President Donald Trump is meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping.

Ahead of that meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in China, Trump said both he and Xi want to see an end to the Ukraine war.

EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10 Published 9 hours ago

Trump says summit with Xi and Putin in China is 'making history'

Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war Published 1 day ago

Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russia says Published 1 day ago

In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace agreement - the government said the UK is also building maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to help Ukraine's war effort.

Burnham, who co-chaired the meeting, had said the UK must do everything it can to make sure Ukraine can defend itself from Russian attacks throughout the winter.

Speaking at a press conference after the talks, Burnham said the mood of the coalition is "more determined than ever to stay the course" in support of Ukraine.

He welcomed the presence of US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the meeting and described Russia as "perhaps the biggest losers" of the conflict, as he referred to casualties they have suffered.

Burnham said: "This clearly has got to be a moment to move towards peace because of the US involvement that we've seen today and the progress clearly that is being made.

"Europe is ready to enter these negotiations, we are clear about what we will accept and what we won't accept, but we are also clear that we stand with Ukraine today, tomorrow, for as long as it takes, until this unjust war is over."

Before this latest support package was announced, government figures put the amount of support provided by the UK for Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022 at £35.5bn. , external

In recent days, Ukraine has struck oil refineries in southern Russia, and has repeatedly hit the Crimean Bridge - a significant logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

Meanwhile, Russian forces have been focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before winter with attacks on critical infrastructure.

The UK is among a number of countries also supplying Ukraine with lightweight missiles which are being used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

Ukraine's strike rate is now close to 70%, more than double what it was just a couple of months ago, Downing Street said.

The UK also pledged further air defence support this week and sanctioned Russia's 10 major oil producers.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the government was delivering on a promise for more support for Ukraine at the Budget.

"Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes," he said.

Meanwhile, on Friday Burnham will head to Brussels for a UK-EU summit, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

stories.title: Timetable set out for dismantling leasehold system in England and Wales
stories.summary: Under the government's plans, a ban on the sale of most new leasehold flats is expected around 2031.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026

The government has set out a timetable for when the leasehold system in England and Wales will be dismantled.

Under the plans, most new flats - with only limited exemptions - will be sold as commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

The government says a modernised commonhold model is expected to be up and running around 2029, followed by a ban on the sale of most new leasehold flats, expected around 2031.

Meanwhile, a £250 cap on ground rents - the annual fee paid by leaseholders to their freeholder - is expected to come into force in 2028, six months after a new law passes.

Ground rents will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

There are around five million leasehold homes in England and Wales, where people own the right to occupy a property via a lease for a limited number of years from a freeholder.

Under commonhold, there is no ground rent or expiring lease.

On Thursday, the government introduced the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill , external to Parliament.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months, and the measures in the bill will not come into force straight away.

The government says the bill will also make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold.

Under the plans, instead of all leaseholders having to agree before a building can convert, only 50% will have to support the move.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Commons Housing Committee, welcomed the bill but said "leaseholders have been waiting far too long for successive governments to tackle the unfair leasehold system".

She added: "I hope the government will consider accelerating the timetable for introducing the £250 cap on ground rent so that leaseholders can see those savings sooner rather than later."

In an interview with the BBC, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner was challenged over whether the government was moving too slowly on leasehold reform.

In response, she said leasehold was an area "fraught with legal challenge".

She added: "We've got the balance right we believe, making sure that we've done the pre-legislative work, to ensure that we've consulted as much as we need to, so that we can implement these changes."

'Continuous torture cell'

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

Fozia Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

Scotland does not have leasehold tenures, while Northern Ireland has just a handful of leasehold properties.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other other countries around the world, which do not have leaseholds.

Risk of two-tier system

Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.

He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy.

He said: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"

The National Leasehold Campaign welcomed the "landmark legislation", but said: "The true test of these reforms will be whether the millions of existing leaseholders already living under the leasehold system are given an affordable and accessible route to commonhold."

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system

The Residential Freehold Association, which represents the UK's largest freeholders, says the bill is "an unprecedented abuse of property rights".

It says the legislation could wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in ground rents.

Many leaseholders have also complained of high service charges, which they have no control over and must pay for the management and maintenance of their building.

The government says new measures added to the legislation will require building owners to check their condition, plan for works and build up funds ahead of time, helping to reduce the risk of homeowners suddenly facing huge bills for repairs.

Other measures in the legislation include:

Abolishing forfeiture, where leaseholders can be threatened with losing their home over unpaid charges as low as £350

Giving ministers the power to cap excessive permission and administration fees, for things like asking to keep a pet or replace a front door

Making it cheaper and easier to extend a lease or buy the freehold.

Sanae Takaichi cuts lonely figure at airport, a move by China that is being linked to the simmering row over Taiwan

Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.

But there was one exception: Japan ’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi .

The red carpet was rolled out for her arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, but Takaichi, on her first visit to China since taking office just over a year ago, had to make do with a modest guard of honour and a welcome from a relatively junior Chinese government official.

The contrast in hospitality was impossible to ignore. Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he stepped off Air Force One, while Vladimir Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior Communist party official and one of Xi’s closest aides.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , beamed as he walked past rows of women in white shirts and pink skirts while soldiers from the People’s Liberation Army stood to attention, bayonets fixed. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, and the country’s first lady, Kim Hea Kyung, were given similar VIP treatment.

Takaichi, on the other hand, was met off her plane by Zhang Qiyue, China’s former ambassador to Greece, a position below those who greeted other leaders. Zhang, though, does have a connection with Japan: her father, Zhang Shu, was once China’s ambassador in Tokyo.

Many are linking China’s frosty welcome to a simmering row over Taiwan that began shortly after Takaichi made her diplomatic debut at the 2025 Apec summit in South Korea, where she and Xi vowed to build “constructive and stable” relations.

Less than a fortnight later, Takaichi triggered a diplomatic crisis when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan, whose westernmost island, Yonaguni , is just 100km from Taiwan.

Insisting that Japan could exercise its right to collective self-defence – or coming to the aid of an ally, namely the US – Takaichi said Tokyo had to plan for a crisis in the Taiwan strait.

Beijing has not ruled out the use of force to annex Taiwan – a self-governing democracy it regards as a Chinese province – under what it calls “reunification”.

China’s foreign ministry condemned her remarks at the time as “wrongful and dangerous,” while online, many accused Japan’s leader of dragging her country back into prewar militarism.

The dispute soured economic and cultural ties. Beijing warned Chinese citizens not to take holidays or study in Japan , claiming, without evidence, that they would face threats to their safety. Grassroots exchanges were called off and the Chinese releases of Japanese films postponed indefinitely.

Panda diplomacy also took a hit in January, when Xiao Xiao and Lei Lei, a pair of giant pandas that had been kept at Ueno Zoo in Tokyo, departed Japan, leaving the country without one of the animals for the first time since 1972, when Tokyo and Beijing normalised diplomatic ties.

As Xi, Trump and Putin prepared to hold historic three-way talks in Shenzhen on Thursday, Takaichi managed only a cordial handshake and a few words with Xi – another reminder that Japan-China relations have yet to come in from the cold.
